claim: Toxoplasma gondii possesses a limited set of actin-regulatory proteins and relies on only three formins (FRMs) to nucleate and polymerize actin.
source: Toxoplasma gondii possesses a limited set of actin-regulatory proteins and relies on only three formins (FRMs) to nucleate and polymerize actin.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a foundational claim about T. gondii's actin regulatory machinery, supported by the subsequent experimental characterization of the three formins.

claim: FRM2 localizes to the apical juxtanuclear region and participates in apicoplast inheritance.
source: FRM2 localizes to the apical juxtanuclear region and participates in apicoplast inheritance.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2, including localization studies and knockout phenotypes.

claim: FRM3 is restricted to the residual body and maintains intravacuolar cell-cell communication.
source: Restricted to the residual body, FRM3 maintains the intravacuolar cell-cell communication.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated through localization data (Figure 3A) and FRAP experiments showing impaired cell-cell communication in FRM3-KO parasites (Figure 3D-F).

claim: Conoidal FRM1 initiates a flux of F-actin crucial for motility, invasion and egress.
source: Conoidal FRM1 initiates a flux of F-actin crucial for motility, invasion and egress.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by extensive experimental data including FRM1 depletion experiments showing complete blocks in motility, invasion, and egress (Figure 4).

claim: The F-actin flux generated by FRM1 depends on myosins A and H.
source: This flux depends on myosins A and H and is controlled by phosphorylation via PKG (protein kinase G) and CDPK1 (calcium-dependent protein kinase 1) and by methylation via AKMT (apical lysine methyltransferase).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated experimentally in Figure 7, where depletion of MyoH or MyoA affects F-actin accumulation patterns.

claim: The F-actin flux is controlled by phosphorylation via PKG and CDPK1.
source: This flux depends on myosins A and H and is controlled by phosphorylation via PKG (protein kinase G) and CDPK1 (calcium-dependent protein kinase 1) and by methylation via AKMT (apical lysine methyltransferase).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experiments using PKG inhibitor C1 and CDPK1 inhibitor 3MB-PP1, which block F-actin flux (Figure 8B, D).

claim: The F-actin flux is controlled by methylation via AKMT.
source: This flux depends on myosins A and H and is controlled by phosphorylation via PKG (protein kinase G) and CDPK1 (calcium-dependent protein kinase 1) and by methylation via AKMT (apical lysine methyltransferase).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated by experiments showing that AKMT depletion abrogates F-actin flux (Figure 8G).

claim: The F-actin flux is independent of microneme secretion.
source: This flux is independent of microneme secretion and persists in the absence of the glideosome-associated connector (GAC).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated by experiments using TFP1-iKD parasites defective in microneme secretion, which still show F-actin basal accumulation (Figure 8A).

claim: The F-actin flux persists in the absence of GAC.
source: This flux is independent of microneme secretion and persists in the absence of the glideosome-associated connector (GAC).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and shown experimentally in Figure 8G, where GAC-depleted parasites still show F-actin flux.

claim: Toxoplasma gondii is an obligate intracellular parasite responsible for toxoplasmosis.
source: The large phylum of Apicomplexa is composed of thousands of protozoan pathogens of medical and veterinary significance including Toxoplasma gondii and the Plasmodium species responsible for toxoplasmosis and malaria, respectively (Adl et al., 2007; Seeber and Steinfelder, 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations to established literature.

claim: Generation and dynamics of F-actin are critical for apicoplast inheritance in T. gondii.
source: In T. gondii, generation and dynamics of F-actin are known to be critical for apicoplast inheritance (Andenmatten et al., 2013; Jacot et al., 2013), constriction of the basal pole, intravacuolar cell-cell communication (Frénal et al., 2017b; Periz et al., 2017) and gliding motility (Dobrowolski and Sibley, 1996; Drewry and Sibley, 2015; Wetzel et al., 2003) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is stated in the introduction with multiple supporting citations from prior literature.

claim: F-actin is critical for constriction of the basal pole in T. gondii.
source: In T. gondii, generation and dynamics of F-actin are known to be critical for apicoplast inheritance (Andenmatten et al., 2013; Jacot et al., 2013), constriction of the basal pole, intravacuolar cell-cell communication (Frénal et al., 2017b; Periz et al., 2017) and gliding motility (Dobrowolski and Sibley, 1996; Drewry and Sibley, 2015; Wetzel et al., 2003) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: F-actin is critical for intravacuolar cell-cell communication in T. gondii.
source: In T. gondii, generation and dynamics of F-actin are known to be critical for apicoplast inheritance (Andenmatten et al., 2013; Jacot et al., 2013), constriction of the basal pole, intravacuolar cell-cell communication (Frénal et al., 2017b; Periz et al., 2017) and gliding motility (Dobrowolski and Sibley, 1996; Drewry and Sibley, 2015; Wetzel et al., 2003) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: F-actin is critical for gliding motility in T. gondii.
source: In T. gondii, generation and dynamics of F-actin are known to be critical for apicoplast inheritance (Andenmatten et al., 2013; Jacot et al., 2013), constriction of the basal pole, intravacuolar cell-cell communication (Frénal et al., 2017b; Periz et al., 2017) and gliding motility (Dobrowolski and Sibley, 1996; Drewry and Sibley, 2015; Wetzel et al., 2003) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The apicoplast is a plastid-like, secondary endosymbiotic organelle surrounded by four membranes.
source: Present in most apicomplexans, the apicoplast is a plastid-like, secondary endosymbiotic organelle surrounded by four membranes that hosts essential metabolic pathways (McFadden et al., 1996; McFadden and Yeh, 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The apicoplast segregates between two forming daughter cells through the action of myosin F.
source: During parasite division, the apicoplast segregates between the two forming daughter cells through the action of myosin F (MyoF), a motor conserved across the phylum of Apicomplexa (Jacot et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Actin is necessary for apicoplast segregation in both T. gondii and Plasmodium falciparum.
source: Concordantly, actin is necessary for this process in both T. gondii and Plasmodium falciparum (Andenmatten et al., 2013; Das et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: MyoF participates in the trafficking of dense granules.
source: Additionally, MyoF is reported to participate in the trafficking of dense granules (Heaslip et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: F-actin is implicated in intravacuolar cell-cell communication mediated by myosin I.
source: F-actin is also implicated in a unique mode of intravacuolar cell-cell communication (Frénal et al., 2017b; Periz et al., 2017), which is mediated by myosin I (MyoI) and responsible for the synchronicity of parasite division within a given vacuole (Frénal et al., 2017b).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Myosin I is responsible for the synchronicity of parasite division within a vacuole.
source: F-actin is also implicated in a unique mode of intravacuolar cell-cell communication (Frénal et al., 2017b; Periz et al., 2017), which is mediated by myosin I (MyoI) and responsible for the synchronicity of parasite division within a given vacuole (Frénal et al., 2017b).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: The basal pole constriction of parasites is governed by myosin J.
source: Finally, the basal pole constriction of the parasites is governed by myosin J (MyoJ), which also participates in the establishment of cell-cell communication (Figure 1A) (Frénal et al., 2017b).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Gliding motility is powered by the glideosome, a molecular machine conserved across the Apicomplexa phylum.
source: Gliding motility is a prerequisite for host cell invasion, parasite egress and migration across biological barriers and is powered by the glideosome, a molecular machine conserved across the phylum (Frénal et al., 2017a).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: The glideosome is composed of an actomyosin system that promotes rearward translocation of transmembrane adhesins.
source: The glideosome is composed of an actomyosin system that promotes the rearward translocation of transmembrane adhesins attached to the extracellular matrix.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction describing the mechanism of the glideosome.

claim: Micronemal adhesins are discharged apically at the parasite plasma membrane by regulated secretory organelles called micronemes.
source: During motility, the adhesins are discharged apically at the parasite plasma membrane by regulated secretory organelles called micronemes (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction describing the mechanism of motility.

claim: In T. gondii, micronemal adhesins typically assemble in complexes composed of one transmembrane protein associated with one or more proteins exhibiting host cell binding properties.
source: In T. gondii, these micronemal adhesins (MICs) typically assemble in complexes composed of one transmembrane protein associated with one or more proteins exhibiting host cell binding properties (Carruthers and Tomley, 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: TRAP and CTRP participate in sporozoites and ookinetes motility in Plasmodium, respectively.
source: In Plasmodium, the adhesins thrombospondin-related adhesive protein (TRAP) and the circumsporozoite-and TRAP-related protein (CTRP) participate in sporozoites and ookinetes motility, respectively (Dessens et al., 1999; Kappe et al., 1999; Steinbuechel and Matuschewski, 2009; Sultan et al., 1997).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: During invasion, rhoptry neck proteins (RONs) are apically discharged onto the host plasma membrane and assemble with AMA1 to form the moving junction.
source: During invasion, parasite-derived receptors, contained in the rhoptry organelles (rhoptry neck proteins, RONs) are apically discharged onto the host plasma membrane. Upon secretion, the RONs assemble with the microneme protein AMA1 (apical membrane antigen 1) to form the moving junction (MJ) (Besteiro et al., 2011; Lamarque et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The basal translocation of the moving junction by the actomyosin system propels the parasite inside the host cell.
source: The basal translocation of this MJ by the actomyosin system propels the parasite inside the host cell, a process conserved in both T. gondii and Plasmodium (Figure 1B–C) (Riglar et al., 2011; Riglar et al., 2016; Vulliez-Le Normand et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: At the end of invasion, the parasite exhibits a twisting motion sealing the parasitophorous vacuole.
source: At the end of the invasion process, the parasite exhibits a twisting motion (Pavlou et al., 2018) sealing the PV and creating a safe and secluded niche for replication (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: In T. gondii, adhesins are connected to F-actin via the glideosome-associated connector (GAC).
source: In T. gondii, the adhesins are connected to the parasite F-actin via the glideosome-associated connector (GAC) (Jacot et al., 2016) and their rearward translocation is powered by the successive actions of MyoH and MyoA (Graindorge et al., 2016; Long et al., 2017a).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Rearward translocation of adhesins is powered by the successive actions of MyoH and MyoA.
source: In T. gondii, the adhesins are connected to the parasite F-actin via the glideosome-associated connector (GAC) (Jacot et al., 2016) and their rearward translocation is powered by the successive actions of MyoH and MyoA (Graindorge et al., 2016; Long et al., 2017a).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Parasite motility is initiated at the conoid by the action of MyoH.
source: Parasite motility is initiated at the conoid, an apical protruding organelle composed of tubulin fibers, by the action of MyoH, which presumably translocates F-actin and GAC in the confined space between the plasma membrane and the inner membrane complex (IMC) that compose the pellicle in Apicomplexa (Graindorge et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: MyoA, anchored in the pellicle, translocates adhesin complexes to the basal pole of the parasite.
source: MyoA, anchored in the pellicle, takes the relay at the level of the apical polar ring (APR) to translocate the adhesin complexes to the basal pole of the parasite (Figure 1B–C) (Andenmatten et al., 2013; Frénal et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Parasite egress is initiated by the activation of PKG.
source: The signaling events leading to parasite egress from infected cells involve the coordinated stimulation of micronemes exocytosis and activation of the actomyosin system. Egress is initiated by the activation of the cGMP-dependent protein kinase (PKG) (Brown et al., 2017; Brown et al., 2017; Wiersma et al., 2004), a central regulator that is involved in phospholipase C (PLC) and calcium-mediated signaling (Bullen and Soldati-Favre, 2016; Jia et al., 2017; Lourido et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: PKG is involved in phospholipase C and calcium-mediated signaling.
source: Egress is initiated by the activation of the cGMP-dependent protein kinase (PKG) (Brown et al., 2017; Brown et al., 2017; Wiersma et al., 2004), a central regulator that is involved in phospholipase C (PLC) and calcium-mediated signaling (Bullen and Soldati-Favre, 2016; Jia et al., 2017; Lourido et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: PLC produces inositol triphosphate (IP3) and diacylglycerol (DAG).
source: PLC produces inositol triphosphate (IP3), which presumably opens an unknown IP3-sensitive Ca2+ channel (Garcia et al., 2017; Lovett et al., 2002) and diacylglycerol (DAG), which is converted on the inner leaflet of the plasma membrane into phosphatidic acid (PA) via diacylglycerol kinase 1 (DGK1) (Bullen et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: DAG is converted into phosphatidic acid (PA) via diacylglycerol kinase 1 (DGK1).
source: PLC produces inositol triphosphate (IP3), which presumably opens an unknown IP3-sensitive Ca2+ channel (Garcia et al., 2017; Lovett et al., 2002) and diacylglycerol (DAG), which is converted on the inner leaflet of the plasma membrane into phosphatidic acid (PA) via diacylglycerol kinase 1 (DGK1) (Bullen et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: APH binds to PA and mediates microneme exocytosis.
source: The acylated plekstrin homology domain-containing protein APH, located on the microneme surface, binds to PA and mediates microneme exocytosis (Bullen et al., 2016; Darvill et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Release of Ca2+ results in the activation of CDPK1, an essential effector of microneme secretion.
source: On the other hand, release of Ca2+ results in the activation of the Ca2+ dependent protein kinase 1 (CDPK1), an essential effector of microneme secretion (Lourido et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: CDPK3 contributes to microneme secretion in some conditions.
source: In addition, but only in some conditions, a second kinase, CDPK3, contributes to the process (Garrison et al., 2012; Lourido et al., 2012; McCoy et al., 2012; Treeck et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: AKMT selectively affects motility without impairing microneme secretion.
source: In contrast to CDPK1-dependent phosphorylation, lysine methylation mediated by the apical lysine methyltransferase (AKMT) selectively affects motility without impairing microneme secretion (Heaslip et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: AKMT plays a critical role in recruiting GAC at the apical tip of the parasite.
source: Remarkably, AKMT plays a critical role in recruiting GAC at the apical tip of the parasite (Jacot et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: F-actin has been difficult to detect in apicomplexans and was assumed to be maintained predominantly as a large pool of monomers.
source: F-actin has notoriously been difficult to detect in apicomplexans and actin was assumed to be maintained predominantly as a large pool of monomers (Dobrowolski et al., 1997; Mehta and Sibley, 2010; Olshina et al., 2012; Skillman et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Actin chromobodies allowed the detection of F-actin networks mainly accumulating in the residual body of T. gondii.
source: Recently, actin chromobodies (Cb) allowed the detection of F-actin networks mainly accumulating in the RB of T. gondii (Periz et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: All apicomplexans lack the ARP2/3 complex.
source: All the apicomplexans lack the ARP2/3 complex (Gordon and Sibley, 2005), and T. gondii relies on three formins (FRMs) to nucleate and polymerize actin.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: FRM1 and FRM2 are well conserved across the Apicomplexa phylum.
source: FRM1 and FRM2 are well conserved across the phylum, whereas FRM3 is restricted to the subgroup of coccidians and shown before to be dispensable (Daher et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: FRM3 is restricted to the subgroup of coccidians and is dispensable.
source: FRM1 and FRM2 are well conserved across the phylum, whereas FRM3 is restricted to the subgroup of coccidians and shown before to be dispensable (Daher et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Endogenous epitope-tagging of FRM1 and FRM2 revealed different localizations from those obtained using antibodies against bacterially produced FH2 domains.
source: Although FRM1 and FRM2 were both localized at the pellicle using antibodies raised against bacterially produced FH2 domains (Daher et al., 2010), endogenous epitope-tagging of both FRMs revealed different localizations.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction comparing previous and current localization data.

claim: FRM1 is restricted to the apical tip of the parasite.
source: FRM1 is restricted to the apical tip of the parasite (Jacot et al., 2016), a localization more concordant with the apical localization of P. falciparum FRM1 (Baum et al., 2008; Douglas et al., 2018) and its predicted role in generating F-actin apically to initiate motility (Graindorge et al., 2016; Jacot et al., 2016; Long et al., 2017a).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Cb-GFPTy showed strong staining of the residual body and in a juxtanuclear region often overlapping with the apicoplast.
source: Cb-GFPTy showed strong staining of the RB as previously reported (Periz et al., 2017), and in a juxtanuclear region often overlapping with the apicoplast (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: C-terminally Ty-tagged FRM2 at the endogenous locus was found restricted to the apical juxtanuclear region.
source: C-terminally Ty-tagged FRM2 at the endogenous locus was found restricted to the same apical juxtanuclear region (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: In non-dividing parasites, FRM2 always co-localized with the Golgi and only transiently overlapped with the apicoplast.
source: In non-dividing parasites, FRM2 always co-localized with the Golgi and only transiently overlapped with the apicoplast (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2C.

claim: FRM2 remained localized to the juxtanuclear region even in the absence of the apicoplast.
source: Even in the absence of the apicoplast, which can be chemically removed using high doses of anhydrotetracycline (ATc, 4 µg/ml) (Jacot et al., 2013), FRM2 remained localized to the juxtanuclear region (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: During T. gondii tachyzoites division, the apicoplast associates with the duplicated centrosomes to ensure its encapsulation in the growing daughter cells.
source: During T. gondii tachyzoites division, the apicoplast associates with the duplicated centrosomes to ensure its encapsulation in the growing daughter cells (Striepen et al., 2000; van Dooren et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the results with supporting citations.

claim: FRM2 was found concentrated at the edges of the elongating and dividing apicoplast.
source: Concordantly, FRM2 was found concentrated at the edges of the elongating and dividing apicoplast (Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), where the two centrosomes are positioned.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Depletion of MyoF did not affect FRM2 localization.
source: Endogenously tagged FRM2 in a MyoF inducible knockdown (MyoF-iKD) strain confirmed co-localization of the two proteins in this juxtanuclear region and depletion of MyoF did not affect FRM2 localization (48 hr +ATc) (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2E.

claim: FRM2-KO parasites exhibited a defect in apicoplast inheritance.
source: FRM2-KO parasites exhibited a defect in apicoplast inheritance (Figure 2F), while the segregation of the Golgi was unaffected (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The segregation of the Golgi was unaffected in FRM2-KO parasites.
source: FRM2-KO parasites exhibited a defect in apicoplast inheritance (Figure 2F), while the segregation of the Golgi was unaffected (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: About 30% of FRM2-KO vacuoles displayed proper distribution of apicoplast in all parasites.
source: The phenotype was partial; with about ~30% of vacuoles displaying a proper distribution of apicoplast in all the parasites,~50% of the vacuoles showing at least one parasite lacking the apicoplast, and ~20% with all the parasites lacking the apicoplast (resulting from the reinvasion of parasites lacking the apicoplast) (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is stated in the results and quantified in Figure 2G.

claim: FRM2-KO parasites exhibited a significant defect in growth competition assay against a GFP expressing wt strain.
source: Consistently, FRM2-KO parasites survived but exhibited a significant defect in growth competition assay against a GFP expressing wt strain, while the parental RH strain was not affected (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2H.

claim: The loss of fitness in FRM2-KO was linked to an intracellular replication defect.
source: This loss of fitness was linked to an intracellular replication defect (Figure 2I).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2I.

claim: In FRM2-KO, the orientation of the daughter cells was altered with increased up/down and down/down orientations.
source: In FRM2-KO, the orientation of the daughter cells was also altered with increased up/down and down/down orientations in contrast to wt parasites where daughter cells predominantly grew side-by-side toward the apical end (up/up) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The apicoplast and few rhoptries but not micronemes accumulated in the residual body of FRM2-KO parasites.
source: The apicoplast and few rhoptries but not micronemes accumulated in the RB (Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 2D.

claim: FRM3 was C-terminally Ty-tagged at the endogenous locus and found weakly expressed, primarily at the basal pole and in the residual body.
source: FRM3 was C-terminally Ty-tagged at the endogenous locus and found weakly expressed, primarily at the basal pole and in the RB (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3A.

claim: During parasite division, FRM3 was detected at the tip of nascent daughter cells in a distinct localization from FRM2.
source: During parasite division, FRM3 was also detected at the tip of nascent daughter cells but in a distinct localization from FRM2 (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Disruption of FRM3 led to no apparent phenotype by plaque assay or competition assay.
source: Disruption of FRM3 was performed by double homologous recombination in RHΔKu80 strain and led to no apparent phenotype by plaque assay or competition assay (Figure 3—figure supplement 2) as previously described with an independent FRM3-KO mutant (Daher et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The absence of FRM3 led to asynchronous division of intravacuolar parasites indicative of a cell-cell communication defect.
source: However, the absence of FRM3 also led to an asynchronous division of intravacuolar parasites that was not reported previously and which is indicative of a cell-cell communication defect (Figure 3B–C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3B–C.

claim: Parasites lacking FRM3 failed to recover fluorescence or only recovered it at a very slow rate in FRAP experiments.
source: In contrast, parasites lacking FRM3 failed to recover fluorescence or only recovered it at a very slow rate (Figure 3E–F).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3E–F.

claim: FRM2-KO showed no defect in fluorescence recovery in FRAP experiments.
source: FRM2-KO showed no defect in fluorescence recovery, ruling out a participation of this actin nucleator in cell-cell communication (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B–C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3B–C.

claim: In FRM3-KO parasites, MyoI is no longer present in the residual body but still accumulated at the basal pole.
source: MyoI was C-terminally tagged at the endogenous locus in FRM3-KO parasites and shown to be no longer present in the RB but still accumulated at the basal pole (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3G.

claim: The localization of MyoJ was not affected and the basal pole constriction appeared normal in FRM3-KO parasites.
source: In contrast, the localization of C-terminally tagged MyoJ was not affected and the basal pole constriction appeared normal (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3H.

claim: The positioning of micronemes and rhoptries, the morphology of the mitochondrion, the inheritance of the apicoplast and the duplication of the Golgi were unaffected by the absence of FRM3.
source: The positioning of micronemes and rhoptries, the morphology of the mitochondrion, the inheritance of the apicoplast and the duplication of the Golgi were unaffected by the absence of FRM3 (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: Two independent FRM1-KO clones contained deletions causing out of frame mutations and were severely impacted in all aspects of motility.
source: Despite multiple attempts, we failed to remove the entire FRM1 locus using the two-gRNA approach but managed to isolate two independent clones using a single gRNA. These two clones contained deletions causing out of frame mutations (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B) and were severely impacted in all aspect of motility (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C–E) without affecting intracellular replication.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B–E.

claim: Reverting parasites rapidly emerged after few passages from the initially clonal FRM1-KO population.
source: Remarkably, reverting parasites rapidly emerged after few passages from the initially clonal FRM1-KO population (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Sequencing of the FRM1 locus in revertant sub-clones revealed spontaneous mutations leading to the correction of the frame shift.
source: Several independent sub-clones were isolated and sequencing of the FRM1 locus revealed spontaneous mutations leading to the correction of the frame shift induced by the CRISPR/Cas9 approach (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F.

claim: FRM1-mAID-HA localized at the tip of the parasite and was tightly degraded upon addition of IAA.
source: FRM1-mAID-HA localized at the tip of the parasite as previously reported (Jacot et al., 2016) and was tightly degraded upon addition of indole-3-acetic acid (IAA, auxin) (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Depletion of FRM1 resulted in no lysis plaques.
source: Depletion of FRM1 resulted in no lysis plaques (Figure 4C) and a complete block in host cell invasion, induced egress and gliding motility (Figure 4D–F) while intracellular replication, apicoplast inheritance and cell-cell communication were not affected (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B–D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Depletion of FRM1 resulted in a complete block in host cell invasion, induced egress and gliding motility.
source: Depletion of FRM1 resulted in no lysis plaques (Figure 4C) and a complete block in host cell invasion, induced egress and gliding motility (Figure 4D–F) while intracellular replication, apicoplast inheritance and cell-cell communication were not affected (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B–D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 4D–F.

claim: Intracellular replication, apicoplast inheritance and cell-cell communication were not affected by FRM1 depletion.
source: Depletion of FRM1 resulted in no lysis plaques (Figure 4C) and a complete block in host cell invasion, induced egress and gliding motility (Figure 4D–F) while intracellular replication, apicoplast inheritance and cell-cell communication were not affected (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B–D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B–D.

claim: Depletion of FRM1 resulted in a complete absence of capped-events and a large increase of bound-events in the beads capping assay.
source: Strikingly, depletion in FRM1 resulted in a complete absence of capped-events and a large increase of bound-events. The same result was observed upon GAC depletion with however a large increase of incomplete capping (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 4G.

claim: FRM1 is firmly anchored to the conoid already in growing daughter cells.
